feedback: Surface the 'heavier falls faster' option as a common distractor and explain why it is wrong (the heavier object is also harder to speed up, so both fall at the same rate in negligible air).
When a learner picks 'same rate always' without a condition, flag the flat-paper-in-air counterexample.
For 'no gravity in space,' link back to the Moon drop and the orbit reframe.

If a learner says gravity acts only on heavy things or stops acting underwater, point out that a leaf and a submerged object still have mass and are still pulled toward the Earth's centre; underwater, buoyancy and water resistance act too but gravity has not switched off.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the rule 'same rate when air resistance is negligible, otherwise air resistance slows light non-compact objects', that gravity acts in space and on the Moon, and that gravity acts on ALL objects with mass — light ones and objects in water included, not only heavy things.
learnerActions: Answer predict-which-lands-first questions for pairs of objects under stated conditions (in air vs in a vacuum).
Sequence or match conditions (air vs vacuum, flat vs crumpled, Earth vs Moon) to outcomes.
Answer a short question on whether there is gravity in space / on the Moon and justify the choice.
Decide whether gravity acts on a very light object (e.g. a leaf) and on an object held underwater, and justify why — gravity still pulls on both because they have mass.
Give everyday examples of gravity in action (dropping objects, jumping and coming back down, water flowing downhill) and explain what gravity is doing in each.
activities.title: Retrieval, prediction, and everyday examples
